I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the peculiar way we experience time, and how our relationship with it shifts as we age.

---

**The Elasticity of Time**

I turned thirty not long ago, and something strange happened to my perception of time. Not the typical "time flies" cliché, though that's part of it. Something more unsettling. I started noticing that my memories of five years ago felt closer than my memories of last Tuesday. The recent past had become strangely flat, while older experiences maintained their three-dimensional weight. I could taste the coffee from a morning in 2019 more vividly than whatever I drank this morning.

This isn't unique to me, of course. Psychologists have documented this phenomenon extensively. We encode novel experiences more densely than routine ones, so years full of firsts—first kisses, first jobs, first failures—feel expansive when we look back on them. Meanwhile, a year of commuting and grocery shopping compresses into a single gray smear. The tragedy, if you want to call it that, is that our most memory-rich years are often our most painful ones. The brain doesn't distinguish between "good" novelty and "bad" novelty. It just encodes everything with extra detail when we're struggling to make sense of it.

I think about this when I talk to my grandmother, who is ninety-three. She remembers the dress she wore to a dance in 1947—the fabric, the color, the boy who stepped on her foot and apologized with such elaborate formality. But ask her what she ate for breakfast, and she might guess cereal, or toast, or nothing. The present has become a thin membrane for her, while the past remains thick and navigable. She's not losing her mind; she's losing the present, which was never very memorable to begin with.

There's a temptation to moralize about this. To say we should live more deliberately, seek novelty, break routines, make each day count. I've read those articles. I've made those lists. But there's something exhausting about the imperative to *make memories*, as if experience is primarily a storage problem. Sometimes I want to live in the gray smear. Sometimes the routine is the point—the comfort of repetition, the meditation of familiar tasks. Not everything needs to be encoded. Not everything needs to be retrieved.

What interests me more is the way we narrate time to ourselves. The stories we tell about our own lives, and how those stories change. I've noticed that my memories of childhood are increasingly contaminated by photographs. I can't remember my sixth birthday party without seeing it through the lens of the few Polaroids that survived. The actual sensory experience—if there ever was one separate from the photo—has been replaced. I remember the photograph remembering for me. This makes me wonder what digital natives will experience, those whose entire lives have been documented in high definition. Will they have any unmediated memories at all? Or will the distinction between lived experience and recorded experience collapse entirely?

I suspect it already has, for many of us. I find myself experiencing things *for* the story I'll tell later, or the post I'll make, or even just the internal monologue I'll construct. The present becomes a rehearsal for the future's recollection. This is a form of alienation, I think—though maybe no more alienating than any other way we've historically organized experience. Religious ritual, family tradition, even the simple act of recounting your day to a partner over dinner—all of these shape and filter the raw material of living. The question is whether the filtering happens in service of connection or isolation.

Time also behaves strangely in anticipation. The week before a vacation feels longer than the vacation itself. The month before a dreaded deadline expands with a kind of malevolent elasticity. We're worse at predicting how we'll feel in the future than we think—this is well-established—but we're also worse at predicting how we'll *remember* feeling. I consistently overestimate how much I'll recall of pleasant experiences and underestimate how much I'll recall of unpleasant ones. The unpleasant sticks more than I want to admit. This might be adaptive—pain teaches, pleasure merely rewards—but it makes for a skewed archive. My memory is a library with too many books on suffering and too few on joy.

I've been trying an experiment lately, inspired by some reading on temporal perception. Once a week, I write down three specific sensory details from that day. Not events, not emotions, just textures of experience. The sound of rain on the metal awning outside my apartment. The particular blue of evening light through kitchen windows. The smell of old books in a shop I wandered into without intention. The goal isn't to make these days memorable in the grand sense, but to create anchors in the present, to resist the flattening. It helps, somewhat. Or at least it helps me believe I'm resisting, which may amount to the same thing.

There's a deeper question here about whether time is something that happens *to* us or something we *do*. Physics tells us time is a dimension like space, that the distinction between past and future may be illusory at the fundamental level. But lived experience insists on the arrow. We don't move through space the way we move through time. We can return to a place, but not to a moment. Unless, of course, we count memory as a kind of return—which it is, but a return to a place that has been rebuilt, not preserved. Every memory is a reconstruction, edited by who we are now, what we know now, what we need now.

This is why I find it hard to trust my memories of who I was. The person I was at twenty made decisions that seem opaque to me now, even monstrously stupid. But I have to remind myself that I am judging that person with the accumulated knowledge of a decade. He didn't have that knowledge. He was doing his best with what he had, which included less experience, less failure, less understanding of his own patterns. I try to extend him the grace I hope my future self will extend me. The forty-year-old me will surely find some of my current choices baffling. I can't prevent that. I can only try to make my reasons legible, to leave traces that might survive the editing process.

What I've come to believe, if I believe anything about time, is that the present moment is both infinitely precious and essentially worthless. Precious because it's all we ever actually have. Worthless because it passes before we can fully grasp it, and most of it will be forgotten. The art of living, if there is one, might be holding both of these truths without collapsing into either despair or manic preservation. To be present without demanding that presence be remembered. To let time pass without fighting its passage. To build a life that feels coherent in the living, not just in the telling.

This is hard. I'm not good at it. But I keep noticing things—the way light moves across a wall, the particular silence of a room when everyone else has gone to sleep, the weight of a cat settling against my leg—and I think: this is it. This is what there is. Not the story I'll tell later, not the memory I'll construct, but this immediate, unrepeatable, already-vanishing now. And then it's gone, and I'm writing about it, or thinking about it, or forgetting it, and the next now arrives, equally unrepeatable, equally doomed.

Time wins, always. But we get to play for a while, and the playing is something, even if we can't keep the score.
